issues.legal_issue: Non-payment of rent is not wilful default when the landlord has consented to collect rent in batches of two or three months and the overdue rent is consistent with that practice.
material_facts: The landlords lived away from the premises and collected rent at their convenience rather than every month.
Receipts showed rent had been collected for two months and three months at a time.
Three months' rent was due when the eviction petition was filed.
issues.conclusion: The tenant's three-month non-payment was not wilful default and could not sustain eviction on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, wilful default, rather than mere default, is a ground for eviction. The Court relied on S. Sundaram Pillai & Ors. v. V.R. Pattabiraman & Ors., which distinguished default from wilful default, and referred to Premchand Banka v. A. Vasanthrai Khatod & Ors. It held that where the landlord consents to collecting rent for two or three months at a time, non-payment for three months does not constitute wilful default.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the basis of alleged non-payment of rent.
predicates.landlord_collected_rent_in_batches: The landlord consented to collecting rent for multiple months at a time rather than collecting it monthly.
predicates.overdue_rent_matched_collection_practice: The rent unpaid when eviction was sought covered a period consistent with the landlord's established collection practice.

issues.definition: When eviction is sought for non-payment, a batch-collection practice and unpaid rent consistent with that practice mean the non-payment is not wilful default.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord's prolonged failure to object to a tenant's changed use of premises, followed by raising that change for the first time in an eviction proceeding, supports acceptance of the non-residential use.
material_facts: The premises had been used in part for commercial activity since 1973.
The landlords did not object to that use for seven years.
The landlords first relied on the changed use as a ground for eviction in 1980.
The tenant maintained that mixed use was the basis of the tenancy.
issues.conclusion: In the circumstances, the landlords had accepted use of the premises for purposes other than residential use, so the changed use did not sustain the eviction petition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court inferred acceptance of the non-residential use from the landlords' failure to object for seven years and their raising the matter for the first time when seeking eviction. No earlier case was cited for this conclusion.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and premises_used_for_nonresidential_purposes and landlord_made_no_objection_for_years and change_first_raised_in_eviction

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant from premises whose use was disputed.
predicates.premises_used_for_nonresidential_purpose: The tenant used the premises, at least in part, for purposes other than residential use.
predicates.landlord_made_no_objection_for_years: The landlord knew of the non-residential use and did not object to it over a prolonged period.
predicates.change_first_raised_in_eviction: The landlord first relied on the changed use as a ground when seeking eviction.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding, prolonged non-objection to non-residential use followed by first raising the change in the eviction case means the landlord accepted that use.
